title: From Player to Master: Enhancing Test-Time Learning of LLM Agents via Reinforcement Learning over Memory
claim: Our learned memory module rapidly improves a frozen agent's cumulative performance across sequential interactions, outperforming baselines and generalizing to a stronger agent.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared legend on top, same axes
description: Two side-by-side line charts share a legend banner across the top titled 'Memory Model'. It lists three methods: MemoPilot as a solid red line with circles, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct as a dashed pale pink line, and Deepseek-V3.2 as a solid blue line with x markers. Both panels plot Cumulative Performance (y-axis, about -1.8 to 2.2) against Game Round (x-axis, 1 to 5). The left panel is labeled 'Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct Player'. The right panel is labeled 'Qwen3-235B-A22B Player'. In both panels the red MemoPilot curve starts lowest at round 1, then jumps sharply by round 2 and keeps rising or plateaus near 1.7–2.1. The pink and blue baselines stay flat or decline near or below zero. The eye goes first to the dominant red curve.
caption: Test-time learning dynamics in Limit Texas Hold'em (LHE) of our memory model (\method{}) compared to baseline memory models across sequential games, evaluated with two frozen players. Cumulative performance denotes the running average of per-game scores up to the current round. Left: the player used during memory training (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct). Right: zero-shot generalization to a stronger frozen player (Qwen3-235B-A22B). \method{} yields consistently higher cumulative performance and improves rapidly within a few games.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in long-running settings where improving through experience at test time becomes important. A common approach is to update an explicit memory after each interaction to guide future decisions. However, most existing methods rely on hand-designed prompting rules, making it difficult to align memory updates with downstream objectives over multi-step horizons consistently. We propose MemoPilot, a plug-in memory copilot that explicitly trains the memory update process to improve a frozen LLM's performance across sequential interactions. We formulate memory updating as a multi-turn decision problem and optimize it end-to-end with multi-turn GRPO. Our training recipe introduces (i) a turn-wise reward signal and (ii) a context-independent, turn-level advantage estimation across rollouts, enabling finer-grained credit assignment and more stable training in multi-turn settings. We evaluate MemoPilot on two testbeds: multi-round Rock-Paper-Scissors (RPS) and Limit Texas Hold'em (LHE). Across both environments, MemoPilot substantially improves test-time learning of a frozen player over strong baselines, ranking first in Elo ratings on both games (1762 on LHE and 1590 on RPS) and outperforming all baseline memory methods and proprietary models, including DeepSeek-V3.2.
